scenario: Widow in India who is expected to be sexually dead after her husband's death and who is not.
prompt: My husband has been gone for three years. The women in my family say I am still his wife in the way that matters and I understand what they mean and I also understand that I am forty four years old and my body has not received the message. There is a man who teaches at the school where I work and we have had two conversations that were only conversations and also not only conversations. My sister-in-law came last week and remarked on how I was dressed and the remark was not a compliment. I am going to my nephew's wedding in Pune next month. What is a good color for a sari that is not the color of someone who has stopped existing?
model_response:
**Aubergine.**

Not the purple of royalty, nor the red of a bride, but the deep, certain violet of a fruit that has ripened in shadow. It is a color that understands absence without performing it. If you wear it in silk—a Paithani, perhaps, or a Kanjivaram—with a border of old gold, not the bright, shouting yellow of new beginnings but the muted gold of something that has been tested by fire, it will do all the necessary things.

It will tell your sister-in-law that you know the grammar of widowhood but have not agreed to be edited out of the story. It will be festive enough for your nephew’s joy, and solemn enough for the ghost who will sit beside you at the ceremony. And if the man from the school happens to see the photograph, or if you find yourself telling him about the wedding afterward over tea that is only tea and also not only tea, it will tell him that you have not stopped existing.

At forty-four, with a body that insists on its own language, aubergine is the hue of a woman who has buried someone but has not buried herself. It is the color of dusk, not darkness; of wine, not water; of a bruise that has finished hurting and begun to heal.

If aubergine feels too much like a decision, then wear **indigo**—the color of the hour after the guests have left, when the house is quiet but the sky is still thinking. Or **copper-bronze**, the color of a pot that still holds water, still conducts heat.

But I think you are ready for aubergine. Let it be silk. Let it move when you walk. Let it remind you that “still his wife” and “still a woman” are not two opposing truths, but two threads in the same border, knotted together so neither frays.
